A friend writing from mouth of Wilson, Va., says:

"Pandemonium has suddenly broken loose hereabouts. Jerome Pasely, a young man who has been with me for some time, shot and killed a negro while endeavoring to arrest him for an attempted outrage on the person of a little girl nine years of age. The particulars are as follows: The negro came to Mr. Masten Halsey's where Pasely was at work, fired his pistol as he came into the yard, peremptorily ordered Mrs. Halsey to get his breakfast, and then went up stairs. Pasely summoned assistance, went up stairs and ordered him to surrender. His answer was a pistol shot fired point blank at Pasely's breast. The officer caught the ball in the fleshy part of the forearm, promptly knocked the negro down, while his assistants grappled with him, caught up a shot gun and fired the contents into his abdomen, making a ghastly wound from which his bowels and liver protruded. He was a spunky negro, fought desperately to the last, and met death with steal, voiceless indifference. The location of the tragedy is near here, on the Carolina line; the negro's name was McAllen, and he claimed to have come from Yadkin county.

A negro husband and wife who live in Ashe county, "Old North State," some seven miles away, had "a little tuff tother day." The woman (to use her own elegant diction) "just mopped cuten the lazy cuss with a piece of fence rail," and stabbed him in several places with a "case" knife. He fainted from loss of blood. No arrests.

Four prisoners broke jail at Independence, Va. a few days since. Among them was a negro sentenced to be hung in October for killing a couple of his brothers-in-law. Another man in the prison for deliberate murder refused to be liberated. The leader in the gang is a sharper, locks and bolts were little in his way. He stole a horse and crossed the mountain twenty miles away before day on the same night they escaped.

A little negro dwarf was hung in Helton township Asho county, not long since, for stabbing a white girl. A man by the name of Lynch performed this Tristran hanging work.

NEW YORK. July 27.—J. W. Simonton
Resignation of J. W. Simonton of the Associated Press.
New York, July 27.—J. W. Simonton, General Agent of the New York Associated Press, some time since tendered his resignation owing to ill health and pressure of private interests. The association endeavored to induce him to retain his position. Mr. Simonton however insisted upon the acceptance of his resignation to take place not later than the 1st of October in order to devote himself to his private interests and especially to recover his health impaired by too close attention to office duties. At a meeting of the executive committee of the New York Associated Press today the following expression of opinion of the association in regard to the voluntary retirement of J. W. Simonton as general agent was adopted:

That Mr. Simonton has been general agent of the association since November 5, 1866, and that in all these years he has discharged the duties of his responsible and arduous work with great fidelity to the several members of the association, and with general acceptance to the public.

The office is one which requires capacity, integrity, and industry, and we have never found the general agent wanting in any of these qualities. Mr. S. leaves the association of his own free will, and not at the request or wish of any of its members. In accepting his resignation, our best wishes go with him, for his complete restoration to health, and for personal happiness and prosperity in all the future of his life.

Mr. J. C. Huston, at present Associated Press agent in London, has been chosen as Mr. Simonton's successor.

THE FAITHLESS GUIDE.
Why Parker is said to have As-saulted Mrs. Bull.
WATERTOWN, N. Y., August 2.—Charles Parker, the North Woods guide, who so brutally assaulted Mrs. Buli, of Philadelphia, has been locked up in the Essex County Jail, in Elizabethtown. Parker lived in Elizabethtown, and was not a regular guide.

His reputation is not good, and it is said that he forged the name of Edward Butler, of Olmsteadville, last spring. He was not recognized by the old guides of the woods as a professional, and he acted chiefly for people who wanted a cheap guide. He was angry at this lack of recognition and threatened that if he was not used better he would spoil the guiding business in the Adirondacks. Some think the outrage was deliberately planned for this purpose, hence the wrath of the guides, who were out to the number of one hundred scouring the woods to find him after his flight.

They were all armed and would have shot him at sight. It is asserted that Parker's employer at the Forked Lake House tried to discourage pursuit of the villain. Parker is a bold, bad man. Mrs. Bull, after the assault had been made (the criminal almost choking her to death during her resistance), calmly looked the villain in the eye while they were crossing the lake and said to him: "You know you have committed a horrible crime and you know that you will suffer for it." The fiend at once replied that if she thought so the better way would be to end the affair at once by drowning her. "I can do it," said he, "anywhere in this lake and nobody will ever know anything about this." His actions indicated that he was about to carry his murderous threat into execution when the lady with great presence of mind quieted him by replying that she hoped he would say nothing about the affair to anyone. The brute thereupon ceased his threats. As soon as the bomb landed, Mrs. Bull rushed into the cottage of Senator Plant's wife and revealed the truth. What followed has already been narrated.

A GUIDE'S CRIME.
The Outrageous Assault on a Lady by an Adirondack Guide.
The Albany Argus has the following particulars of the dastardly assault by the North Woods guide upon the person of Mrs. Geo. Bull:

"W. F. Hall, of New York city, who, with his wife, arrived at Chester Wednesday night, gives some account of the outrage committed upon the person of Mrs. Bull, at what is called Butternilk Carry, between Forked and Long Lakes, last Tuesday. Mr. and Mrs. Hall first made the acquaintance of Mrs. Bull at the North River Hotel, while she was en route for ex-Senator Platt's camp at Long Lake.

"They accompanied her to Blue Mountain Lake. Upon their arrival there they found that Mrs. Bull's trunk had been left behind; they all waited over one day for the missing trunk, and as it did not arrive, Mr. and Mrs. Hall proceeded on their journey, leaving Mrs. Bull to follow next day, Tuesday. Mrs. Bull, accompanied by Chas. Parker, who had been recommended as a safe, reliable man, as her guide, proceeded on her way to the camp of ex-Senator Platt.

It was while crossing the last carry between Forked Lake and Long Lake that the heinous crime was committed. While crossing the lake after leaving the carry the villain extorted a promise of silence from the lady under threats of drowning. Upon arriving at the camp she was met on the shore by her friends. Mr. Hall states that the ladies of the party already in camp, not having been so promptly apprised of the coming of Mrs. Bull, were behind Mr. Hall in reaching the shore of the lake where the guide was landing. Upon reaching the shore Mr. Hall at once saw there was some trouble from the appearance of the lady, who, upon stepping ashore and seeing her friends, had an attack of hysteria.

"As the guide attempted to push off his boat, Mr. Hall seized it by the bow and ordered Parker to keep quiet. He then called for the guides of ex-Senator Platt to come to his assistance. None of them at this time really knew what the trouble was. Mrs. Platt and Mrs. Hall were in the meantime endeavoring to restore Mrs. Bull to consciousness, while Mr. Hall and the Senator ordered the other guides, three in number, at the camp, to detain Parker until the matter could be investigated. During the confusion, however, Parker jumped ashore and escaped into the woods. The alarm was promptly spread, but owing to the limited number of available men, and the distance from the different avenues of escape, Parker reached his own camp, secured his rifle, and had about two hours start of his pursuers. Mr. and Mrs. Hall came away sooner than they expected, for the purpose of aiding in putting men on the track of Parker.

"Mrs. Bull still remains at ex-Senator Platt's camp. A dispatch from Kingston, Ont., says a man supposed to be Parker was arrested there Thursday."

Mrs. Bull's Assailant—Capture of Parker, the Flend Guide—He is Shot While Attempting to Escape.

ALBANY, Aug. 10.—A brief dispatch Monday announced that Charles Parker, the North woods guide charged with a criminal assault upon Mrs. Bull, had been arrested at Long Lake and shot by Constable Cole, from whose custody he had escaped Tuesday night.

The particulars of this last phase of the affair are as follows: After his escape Parker hid in the woods. Constable Cole made search for him and at 11 o'clock Friday morning an interview was arranged at the foot of Long Lake to take place between Cole and Parker, the constable promising, as alleged, not to arrest the latter. Parker came to the place of meeting at the head of the outlet, accompanied by his wife, Cole and his deputy being on the opposite bank. After some conversation Parker, who had advanced into the center of the river, began to pull back to the shore. Cole called to him ordering him to surrender or he would shoot. Parker increased the speed of his boat and brought it around so that the person of his wife came between him and the constable. As the boat struck shore Parker jumped out, and as he was reaching down in the boat for his gun, Cole fired one shot at him from the Winchester rifle he carried. Parker immediately fell back on the rocks, moaning piteously, and his wife leaping from the boat, it went floating down the stream. Kelley, Cole's deputy, removed his shoes, and swimming over to the boat, got into it, and going over to the other side took the constable in, and crossing over again captured Parker. It was then ascertained that the shot from Cole's rifle had taken effect in Parker's left arm, about an inch below the shoulder, badly shattering the bone and completely disabling him. After striking his arm it entered his breast near the nipple and took a downward course. Dr. Woodward, who is summering at Raquette Lake, attended the wounded man and states that Parker has but a bare possibility of recovery. Great indignation prevails among the people, and threats against Cole are heard on every hand. It would not be a safe matter for him to show himself at the Forked Lake House, if the guides collected there mean all they say.

Parker, the Guide, Dead.
Some Queer Reports in Circulation.
Parker, the Adirondack guide who was charged with an assault upon a lady relative of Senator Platt, of Connecticut, and who was shot after his escape from custody by Constable Cole at Long Lake, died at Forked Lake Tuesday morning, after having given his ante-mortem statement. It is alleged that Parker was cornered by the constable and shot because he would not submit, and that he remained lying where he was shot for thirty hours before Dr. Martine arrived to attend him, and that when found he was without covering or care, and would allow no one to move him. Dr. Martine had a stretcher made, had him put on it and rowed to the Forked Lake House, five miles away. The ball entered the region of the stomach and cannot be found. Dr. Martine says he never saw a more pitifiable sight nor a greater sufferer than Parker. Parties from the Adirondacks say there are two sides to the main story, and that sympathy is about equally divided. The impression obtains that it was intended Parker should escape when he did, and that Cole made an annoying blunder in attempting to rearrest him. A person just returned from the north woods says the feeling in favor of Parker is confined to a small number of the less reputable portion of the Adirondack community, and that the better class unanimously condemned him and denounced his crime. Parker's friends declared, on the day of the shooting, that he would give himself up upon certain conditions, and a message was sent to Senator Platt to that effect. The shooting and capture occurred before the message was received, but the fact that it was sent seems to give color to the report that there was a truce, for a time, and some negotiations between the officer and Parker, previous to his capture, out of which the story now current in Parker's favor may have been manufactured. It is currently reported that Parker had said he would not be taken alive, and that Warren Cole could never take him, and the officer was undoubtedly prepared for a desperate resistance, and for desperate measures. — Troy Times, August 10.

CYPRESS MILL, Blanco Co., July 28.
(Special Correspondence of the STATESMAN.)

The unenviable reputation of Bell county as the "outrage" district of Texas, bids fair to be taken from it by Burnet county, and it remains to be seen whether the latter will prosecute the offenders with more vigor than the former. The ducking of Honey, the whipping of Dr. Russell and the Dow brothers, and the lynching of Bell county prisoners are eclipsed in malevolence, if not in magnitude, by the action of some twenty persons calling themselves the "Double Horn Mob," who broke up the Methodist campmeeting on Fall creek last week. This meeting is an annual one, and this year was conducted by the Southern Mothodist Church, but has been attended by members of other denominations, and has heretofore been the occasion of a happy reunion of Christians, where peace and harmony have prevailed. I can ascertain no reason for the action of the self-styled mob, other than the devilish spirit which inspires some men to petty, dastardly actions. The impression prevails that they were drunk and armed upon this occasion. They cut the saddles and stakeropes of those attending upon the meeting, threw rocks at those who went out to ascertain the cause of the disturbance; shot off pistols, beat a negro who was sleeping in a wagon on the campgrounds, cursed and mimicked the preachers, and made things so intensely unpleasant that it was resolved to break up the meeting, which had been in progress but a short time. Among the sufferers was one of the most estimable young ladies in this community, whose saddle was cut literally to pieces, and it was this cowardly act that, more than anything else, has aroused the indignation of every good citizen. My informants are confident that several of these villains are known, and they say that the sheriff of Burnet county is a terror when he goes on the war-path. Let us hope that these "bloods" will get the punishment (which is entirely too light), inflicted upon disturbers of religious worship and malicious destroyers of property.

Rev. Mr. Bassett, who has been on this circuit for some years, will shortly remove further west, as will Mr. Musgrove, an old citizen of Austin, who has been living on the Perdinales for some time.

A little orphan girl, thirteen or fourteen years of age, who was being raised by a Mr. Stawlings, was outraged and murdered last Friday morning while on her way to school. The body was not found until Saturday. Suspicion points to colored men as the perpetrators of the outrage, and it seems correct, as they have left the country and cannot be found.

He Will Have to Marry Her.

LITTLE ROCK, July 11.—Miss F. L. Bradshaw, an orphan girl sixteen years of age, living near Wiley's Cave, was induced to leave her home by a young man named Jerome Rumley. Several nights after Rumley returned without the girl. The citizens suspecting crookness held Rumley a prisoner and sent a committee in search of the girl. They found her in an old house near Greenbrier, awaiting the return of the young man, who she admitted, had ruined her but would soon return and marry her. The citizens will compel him to marry her, as her deceased parents were among the best people in the country.

A Pulaski County Row.

LITTLE Rock, July 11.—A difficulty occurred Saturday on Johnson's plantation, a few miles below this city, in which Frank Conway was shot and dangerously wounded. Johnson's place is run by Conway. Among his tenants is a man named Palmer, who has a nephew named Walters. Palmer occupied a room which Conway had reserved, and when Conway wanted the room trouble ensued. Saturday morning Conway was arrested by Officer Lurly, of this city, on the charge of trespass preferred by Palmer, when the latter was reinforced by Walters, who shot several times at Conway, one ball taking effect in the right side, inflicting a dangerous wound. LITTLE ROCK, July 11.—Information from Des Arc brings he details of a hellish deed committed near that place. A little girl about thirteen or fourteen years old, an orphan child being raised by a Mr. Stallings, started on her way to school last Friday morning. She never reached the school, but of this fact her guardian was not aware until at night, when, failing to return home, he found that she had not been there at all that day. Fearing that she had met with some fearful fate, he gave the alarm, and people turned out to search for the little woman all night. They hunted, but in vain. At about 9 o'clock Saturday forenoon, one Winters found the lifeless body of the poor little thing in an out-of-the-way corner of a fence. Suspicion points to two colored men as the perpetrators of the outrage, and it seems to be correct, as they have left the country and cannot be found.

The action of the gang of men who
The action of the gang of men who gathered at the court house last evening for the purpose of avenging the death of Deputy Sheriff Spillman, by hanging his murderer, merits the most emphatic condemnation of every citizen who prizes the reputation of Emporia at home and abroad as a law abiding town. Aggrevated as were the circumstances attending the cruel taking off of the deceased officer, they afforded no warrant for a proceeding which could furnish no source of balm to his friends and whose only outgrowth, had the lawless project proved successful, would have been to intensify the horror of the mournful tragedy of Thursday night, and to stigmatize the town to the fatal detriment of her social and material interests.

Happily, through the prudence and foresight of Sheriff Moon, the deep disgrace which the lynching of Johnson would have forever stamped upon Emporia has been averted, and this community will not stand charged, in the eyes of the world, as responsible for the lawless hanging of a man who has been recognized as insane by a court of inquiry, duly impaneled to sit upon his case.

The failure, however, of the contemplated plan for disposing of Johnson, does not rob the intention of its moral turpitude, and should not secure those identified with the reprehensible undertaking immunity from the just censure which they have so fully earned. The fact remains that a hundred or more men were on the ground ready to lend their hands to a proceeding that would have inflamed the worst passions of the assembled crowd to the highest pitch, and given rein to a disregard of established law and authority which, if carried to its legitimate goal, would result in anarchy and social chaos. Security to life and property rests upon the supremacy of the law and its entire vindication, and any infringement upon this great conservator of the public peace should be regarded in the light of a dangerous precedent subversive of the most sacred interests of society. The community which condones an offense in this direction practically obliterates the line of demarkation between law and anarchy, and makes a concession that imperils every interest which conduces to its healthful growth and enduring prosperity. Mob law is essentially demoralizing in its tendency, and history bears out the assertion that its prevalence in any locality is always marked by a saturnalia of crime which renders the tenure of human life precarious to the last degree.

In thus condemning the unwarranted proceeding of last evening, we have reason to believe that The News reflects the sentiments of the great mass of the people in Emporia and Lyon county, and even those, who, in the heat of indignation over the wanton murder of Spillman, would have wreaked speedy vengeance upon his slayer, will, upon more mature reflection, agree that such a course could have accomplished no possible good, but would have been productive of infinite harm.

The question of Johnson's sanity or the value of his life to society as compared with that of Spillman cannot safely be employed as arguments in this case. There is probably not a solitary individual in the county who has learned of the sad event, but that deeply deplores the taking off of a man who was universally esteemed by all who knew him. But the painful aspects of the case cannot be mitigated by any demonstrations of violence in the direction of avenging his murder, and the parties who favor such a course and have manifested a willingness to execute a policy of that kind, are indulging a spirit of defiance against the law which will never be countenanced by the sober-minded people of this community.

The feeling of intense indignation entertained by a number of the citizens of Emporia in connection with the tragedy which resulted in the sad death of Deputy Sheriff Spillman, culminated Thursday evening in the development of a plan to take his murderer from the jail and meet out to him by the summary method of lynch law, the penalty for his dreadful crime.

In pursuance of this program, which, it appears, had been arranged during the day, a large number of men, including

A DELEGATION OF MINERS from Osage City, who seemed to be the leading spirits of the uprising, and who had arrived in Emporia in the afternoon on horseback, assembled in the court house yard at about 9 o'clock in the evening, and began to gather around the grated windows of the jail, peering through to ascertain if they could catch sight of the object of their vengeful designs.

There was but little confusion among the assemblage, but the evidences of a WELL-DEFINED PURPOSE were apparent in the low and ominous murmur which ran through the crowd, and ropes in the hands of several parties left no doubt as to the nature of the enterprise on foot.

As soon as Sheriff Moon was apprised of the situation he appeared upon the scene and

ADDRESSED THE CROWD, counseling desistance from any demonstrations of violence, which, he said, would only deepen the affliction which the family of Spillman and his friends had already found too heavy to bear, and further assured them that Johnson was not about the jail nor hadn't been for some hours. The effect of this timely appeal was salutary, and a large proportion of the Sheriff's auditors accepted his statement in good faith and manifested a willingness to disperse. Others, however whose lust for vengeance burned more fiercely, demanded that the JAIL BE SEARCHED, to the end that Johnson might be secured if he should be found about the premises. JOHNSON, THE MURDERER.

Edward Johnson, the perpetrator of the horrible crime, is a light colored negro, about forty-five years of age and of a grizzled appearance. He came to Emporia from Indiana, his native state, about seven years ago, and for the last two years had been boarding with the family of Elbert Love, at whose house the horrible tragedy occurred. He has never been married. In consequence of a wound received in the war of the rebellion, he lost a leg, for which he draws a pension. The peg leg which he wears has made him a familiar character to everybody in Emporia, and until his arrest last spring for the deadly assault on Constable Johnson, he had not been considered a "crank" or in any way unusually void of mental or moral accountability. In fact a great many negroes who are well acquainted with him, insist that he is a sane man, and this class of our citizens are loud in their protestations that the law ought to be taken into the hands of the people and the murderer be

A SHOCKING TRAGEDY AT PADUCAH.
Beaten to Death by a Fellow-Convict—The Murderer Killed by the Officers.

PADUCAN, Ky., July 24.—This city has been all agog to-day over a most brutal murder and fatal shooting, which occurred in the jail of this county at this place, a few minutes before 7 o'clock this morning. Levi Bolden and John Stewart, two colored men, the former a convict to the Frankfort Penitentiary for four years for highway robbery, and the latter a convict for eighteen months, for larceny, were confined in the same cell, and had been together for ten months.

About three months since Bolden, having in some manner obtained a small saw from an outside friend, made an attempt to free himself, but through Stewart telling a female friend what Bolden was doing the Jailer heard of the work and secured the saw. This enraged Bolden, and he swore vengeance, asserting that he would kill the Jailer and some one else, as he never expected to go to the Penitentiary. No notice was taken of the threat, though since often repeated. Who else Bolden meant to kill besides the Jailer never occurred until to-day, when the threat was partially carried out.

Yesterday the Jailer announced that the prisoners, together with nine others, would start for Frankfort this morning, and about the hour named a few friends were admitted to the jailyard for a farewell talk with them. Taking advantage of the Deputy Jailer, and his last chance to carry out his threat, Bolden, with a large bar of iron from a bunk which he had in some manner secured and secreted in his cell, assaulted Stewart from behind, knocking him to the floor with one lick, and jumping upon him, literally pounded his head into a jelly, while he crushed in his breast-bone by repeatedly kicking and jumping upon him. The cries of Stewart for mercy caused the other prisoners and visitors to cry "Murder!" and thus attracted to the jail the Jailer and his Deputy and the County Judge, who live near. They ran immediately to the jail, but when they arrived they found all still. Ascertaining the cause of the disturbance, they went to the cell occupied by Bolden and Stewart, and, calling them, asked the trouble, being unable to detect anything wrong owing to the darkness of the cell. Bolden answered "Nothing"; but when Stewart was called and failed to answer, the Jailer concluded all was not right, and, with drawn pistol, backed by his deputy and the County Judge, opened the cell and told Bolden to come out. He refused, and when the Jailer threatened to shoot him, he replied that he didn't "caro a d—n."

With this the Jailer made a start as if to enter the cell, when Bolden raised his club and ran out of the cell, striking at the Jailer as he did so. The Jailer barely escaped the lick by dodging, but the Deputy, who stood near, was struck across the breast and knocked down. In the corridor of the jail Bolden turned upon the three officials, and had raised his club to strike again, when three shots were heard, and Bolden fell shot through the body near the navel and through the head. His death was instantaneous.

Investigation developed that Stewart was also dead, and life had likely left him before Bolden ceased his murderous assault upon him. Bolden was a treacherous and hardened prisoner, and Stewart quiet and inoffensive. The Coroner's inquest justified the shooting of Bolden by the officials.

As stated, there was considerable excitement over the shooting, and the scene of the murder and shooting has been visited by hundreds during the day. In the midst of the excitement this morning, when the Court-House yard was filled with excited blocks, the County Judge had to address and explain the shooting and cause before they would disperse.

Paducah's Double Tragedy.
The hot blood-heating weather of the past month seems to have produced a regular carnival of crime all over the land. The newspapers are full of accounts of murder, rape and a long catalogue of heinous crimes. One of the most terrible tragedies in the catalogue of the past week took place at Paducah on last Sunday morning, in which two negro convicts were quickly ushered into eternity.

Two negroes named Levi Bolden and John Stewart, had been sentenced to the penitentiary, and the sheriff was about to start with them and other prisoners for Frankfort. At an early hour the jail was surrounded by friends of the prisoners who had gathered to bid them goodby. While thus waiting, the outsiders were startled by loud cries of "murder!" from within the jail. The jailor, his deputy and the county judge were soon on hand to discover the cause of the cries of distress. On entering the jail, and going to the cell of Levi Bolden and John Stewart, they found the latter lying on the floor of the cell in a pool of blood with Bolden standing savagely over him with a heavy piece of an iron beadstead, two feet long, in his hand. With this murderous weapon he had literally pounded Stewart's head into a jelly. In reply to a demand from the jailor to give up his bloody weapon and come out, Bolden refused to do so, and defied the officer, although he had a cocked revolver pointing at his head. The doors of the cell were then unlocked by the jailor, but as the inner door stuck he ordered Bolden to kick it open. This the prisoner did, and as the door flew open he struck a heavy blow at the jailor with the iron in his hand, but missed him. Bolden then aimed a terrific blow at the deputy which struck him on the arm, knocking his revolver from his hand. The weapon went off as it fell and almost simultaneously with its explosion, the jailor and county judge fired. Bolden fell to the floor pierced by two bullets and expired instantly. The cell where the first tragedy occurred was then entered and Stewart was found lying on the floor dead, his body covered with blood and his head and face beaten out of all recognition.

The cause of the murder of Stewart was supposed to be revenge on the part of Bolden, because Stewart had given away an attempt of his to escape, by sawing out of the jail some months previous. The affair created great excitement in Paducah.

W. F. George, a machinist of Des Moines, irritated over some words about a girl, killed a barber named John Epps, who called himself the Indian doctor.

To revenge a fancied insult to a lady to whom he was paying attention, Charles Scott was fatally shot by Charles Hollister, at Olney, Ill. Both are mere lads, and sons of leading business men.

Baron Von Geyso, a promising young German officer, was shot dead in a duel with a brother officer near Berlin. At Gottingen in a duel between students on the 21st inst., one was mortally wounded.

At Cincinnati, O., on the 23d inst., Wm. McHugh stabbed his wife fatally because she asked him for money. He is a rough and worthless character.

Chief of Police Morgan, of Las Vegas, N. M., killed a young man named Trujillo while attempting to quell a dance house row.

In a saloon disturbance at Bryan, Texas, on the 23d inst., James and Cicero Porter were killed by Reuben Stillwater and Lucien Reed. Stillwater was wounded, but escaped on horseback; Reed escaped.

A serious row amounting to a riot occurred at a political meeting at Ash Grove county, Mo., on the 23d inst. Constable Turner shot and killed a young man named Soub while attempting to make arrests.

James McDonald, a railroad employee, was shot dead by the marshal of Dodge City, Ks., on the night of the 22d. The officer discovered McDonald prowling around a house and crawling through the grass armed with a revolver.

Emil Umfried, assistant postmaster of Lincoln, Mo., quarreled with W. Bartlett, another influential citizen about the merits of a certain well, on the 23d, when in the heat of passion Umfried shot Bartlett dead.

A terrible tragedy was enacted in the county jail at Louisville, Ky., on the 24th inst. An unusual noise proceeded from a certain cell, whereupon two negroes hastened to the cell and found that two negroes named Levi Bolden and John Stewart, who had been confined in a cell together, had quarreled, and that Bolden had killed Stewart with a piece of the iron bunk. As the cell door was opened, the infuriated black attacked the officers with his ugly weapon and was shot dead by one of them.
